question: Which retained and allocated memory sources dominate parser execution on the frozen production corpus, and how much of the process high-water mark is generated DFA cache, parse-tree and token retention, or runtime overhead?
hypothesis: Generated DFA caches account for most retained heap after a cache-reuse pass, while per-file parse trees and token streams are released and contribute comparatively little retained memory; ATN and DFA closure allocation dominates allocation volume.
selection: Full 1,244-file opaque corpus, the 311-file largest byte-size quartile, and the 12-file highest median parser-core tail from experiment 004.

profilers.typescript: Node.js with --expose-gc and an 8 GB old-space cap; forced-GC retained deltas after clearing decision DFAs; staged parse-tree, source, and token-stream drops; inspector sampling heap profiler at 32 KiB; per-file DFA state counts.
profilers.java: Temurin 21 in Docker; forced-GC retained deltas after clearDFA; staged drops with the parser removed before the tree; jcmd GC.class_histogram -all; ThreadMXBean allocated bytes; /proc/self/status VmHWM.

config.repeats: 2 for q4 and tail; 1 for the full corpus
config.selection: reused from experiments/003 and experiments/004; selection fingerprint must match the latency campaign
config.overhead: one uninstrumented pass per adapter and selection; instrumented cost is reported separately

acceptance: Major retained-memory and allocation sources are quantified with evidence.
DFA cache growth, parse-tree/context retention, token storage, and runtime overhead are distinguishable where tooling permits.
At least one repeat verifies the dominant allocation result.
No optimization is proposed solely from RSS observations.
Published artifacts contain no private path, source text, object name, or original identity.
limitations: V8 heap snapshots were rejected: a 12-file tail snapshot was 2.7 GB and exceeded in-process read limits; forced-GC deltas replace snapshot attribution.
The Node memory harness uses an 8 GB old-space cap, which changes GC thresholds relative to the default production run.
The Java class histogram reports shallow live bytes by class; arrays and hash maps are not attributed to a parser owner.
Sampling allocation bytes are estimates; Java thread allocation bytes are cumulative allocation, not retained memory.
Forced garbage collection and allocation sampling change wall time; instrumented results are not production benchmarks.
One representative file isolates tree, source, and token retention; it is not a corpus average.
No optimization follows from this experiment without a paired control and candidate campaign.
